narrative:
The model estimated an 83.6% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. That is a high-risk estimate, not a certainty, but it is why your law-school application was denied: the decision treated that elevated risk as too great.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the first decile, while admitted students averaged near the sixth decile, and this factor pushed the prediction most strongly toward bar-exam failure. Your first-year standing was the second most influential factor and showed the same pattern: first decile versus an accepted-student average near the sixth decile, again pushing toward failure. Family income was the third most important factor, but it worked in the opposite direction: coming from an upper-middle-income household slightly pushed toward passing, and this group is common among admitted students. It was not enough to offset the academic-standing signals.

To improve your chances, meet with admissions and academic support to understand how your record is evaluated. Ask what evidence could address the bar-risk concern, such as a stronger LSAT retake after preparation, additional coursework or credentials, and a clear study plan. Your LSAT of 30 versus an admitted average of 37 and undergraduate GPA of 2.60 versus 3.23 are areas to discuss and strengthen.
